claim: Gyeongbokgung Palace adult admission is 3,000 won; free for those wearing hanbok, under-6, and seniors 65+, and free for everyone on Culture Day (last Wednesday monthly).
quote: Adult tickets cost 3000 won, with 1500 won for children. Children six and younger, seniors 65+, and anyone wearing hanbok get in for free, and admission is free for everyone on Culture Day.

claim: Gyeongbokgung is open 09:00 with seasonal closing (17:00 Nov-Feb, 18:00 Mar-May & Sep-Oct, 18:30 Jun-Aug), closed Tuesdays.
quote: November-February 09:00-17:00, March-May & September-October 09:00-18:00, and June-August 09:00-18:30. The palace is closed on Tuesdays.

claim: Gyeongbokgung's royal changing-of-the-guard ceremony runs at 10:00 and 14:00 daily except Tuesdays, lasting about 20 minutes at Gwanghwamun Gate.
quote: The changing of the guard takes place at 10am and 2pm every day except Tuesdays... continues for about 20 minutes. The ceremony is held at Gwanghwamun Gate.

claim: Changdeokgung's Secret Garden (Huwon) requires an advance-booked guided tour costing 8,000 won for adults (combined with the 3,000-won palace entry), as daily visitor numbers are capped.
quote: adults (ages 19-64) cost 8,000 won... The main palace itself costs 3,000 won... entry is only permitted with a guided tour, so you must book a guided tour ticket in advance.

claim: Changdeokgung opens 09:00-17:00 (last entry 16:30, extended to 18:00 in summer) and is closed Mondays; the Secret Garden tour is a mandatory ~90-minute walk booked via royal.khs.go.kr.
quote: Changdeokgung operates from 9 AM to 5 PM... extended hours until 6 PM in summer months. The palace is closed on Mondays... The Secret Garden tour consists of a mandatory 90-minute tour.

claim: N Seoul Tower observatory admission is 29,000 won for adults and 23,000 won for children/seniors (official 2026 rate).
quote: Adults: \29,000" and "Child / Seniors: \23,000

claim: N Seoul Tower is open 10:00-23:00, with the observation deck closing to new visitors 30 minutes before closing.
quote: N Seoul Tower is open from 10:00-23:00. However, the observation deck is closed to new visitors 30 minutes prior to closing.

claim: The Namsan cable car to N Seoul Tower runs 10:00-23:00, takes about 3 minutes, and costs 15,000 won round-trip for adults (11,500 won children).
quote: Adult return tickets are priced at 15,000 won, while children's return tickets are 11,500 won. The Namsan Cable Car takes approximately three minutes to reach the summit.

claim: Gwangjang Market (Seoul's oldest market) is open daily ~08:30-18:00 with food stalls running later, famous for bindaetteok (mung-bean pancake), mayak kimbap, soondae, and hand-cut kalguksu noodles.
quote: famous for authentic street foods such as soondae (pork blood sausage), bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes), mayak kimbap, and hand-cut noodles

claim: Gwangjang Market's lunchtime rush (12:00-14:00) brings long queues; restaurants stay open until 23:00 and Sundays are quieter.
quote: Gwangjang Market is open daily between 8:30 am - 6 pm, though restaurants operate until 11:00pm... The lunchtime rush between 12 pm and 2 pm sees throngs of office workers.

claim: Namdaemun Market, one of Seoul's largest traditional markets, runs roughly 10:00 to 05:00 next-day with some wholesale shops open overnight, known for kalguksu and braised galchi (hairtail).
quote: Namdaemun Market is usually open from 10:00 AM to 5:00 AM the next day, making it one of the few places in Seoul that truly never sleeps.

claim: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), Zaha Hadid's landmark neofuturist building, has free-to-access exterior, plazas and design store; open Tue-Sun 10:00-19:00 and closed Mondays (paid exhibitions vary).
quote: The exterior, Oulim Square, the Dongdaemun History & Culture Park, and the DDP Design Store are all free to access at any time.

claim: Bukchon Hanok Village's residential alleys (notably Bukchon-ro 11-gil) are a managed quiet zone restricting tourist entry before 10:00 and after 17:00, with a 100,000-won fine for violations.
quote: Access to the main residential alleys is strictly prohibited before 10:00 AM and after 05:00 PM... A fine of 100,000 won will be imposed on those who enter the area outside these hours for tourism purposes.

claim: Bukchon Hanok Village is a real residential neighborhood of preserved Joseon-era hanok with cafes and viewpoints, but as of January 2025 non-guests can only enter between 10am and 5pm and must be respectful.
quote: As of January 2025, visitors that aren't staying in guesthouses in the area can only enter between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. ... visitors are advised to be respectful at all times while looking around.

claim: Samcheong-dong offers a quaint, relaxed atmosphere on the hills near Gyeongbokgung, with traditional houses converted into cafes and sloping alleys giving viewpoints over Bukchon.
quote: Samcheong-dong is one of the few neighbourhoods where you can experience a quaint, relaxed atmosphere in a busy city like Seoul. ... many traditional residential houses have been converted into cafés, blending modern aesthetics with historic hanok charm.

claim: Seongsu, the 'Brooklyn of Seoul,' has a chilled-out hipster edge with art galleries, design-focused concept stores, and standout cafes like Daelim Changgo Gallery Cafe; wander for pop-ups.
quote: a chilled-out, hipster edge ... art galleries, coffee shops, stylish eateries, and design-focused concept stores ... Daelim Changgo Gallery Cafe – described as 'iconic' with rotating art installations ... 'just wander and see what you find.'

claim: Seongsu evolved from a gritty industrial area into a creative 'newtro' neighborhood, with factory-conversion cafes (Cafe Onion, Grandpa Factory), Brooklyn-inspired bars (Sound Planet), and Common Ground, the world's largest shipping-container mall.
quote: Cafe Onion Seongsu is in a gutted 1970s building that served as a former factory ... Sound Planet is a self-described Brooklyn-inspired bar ... Common Ground is the largest shipping container mall in the world, comprised of 200 shipping containers

claim: Euljiro ('Hipjiro') is a half-gentrified old-town district where crumbling warehouses host hidden craft-cocktail speakeasies with no signage (The Fountain, Bonvivants), alongside pojangmacha alley street-drinking, best after 8pm.
quote: crumbling warehouse walls coexist with minimalist coffee shops ... many bars don't have visible signage and operate by word-of-mouth ... 'Euljiro Pojangmacha Alley' near Euljiro 4-ga Station offers 'total local Korea'

claim: Euljiro earned the nickname 'Hip-jiro' in the mid-2010s as trendy cafes and bars opened in old buildings; popular hip bars include George Tunnel, Euljiromun and Dongbaek Palace, and the alleys turn hippest after the hardware shops close at night.
quote: trendy cafes and bars renovated from old buildings started opening one after another, earning the area the new nickname 'Hip-jiro' ... 'George Tunnel', 'Euljiromun', 'Dongbaek Palace', and 'Hip-jang' are especially popular.

claim: Hongdae, centered on Hongik University, is Seoul's youth-culture and indie hub with buskers, the 'Walking Street' (Eoulmadang-ro), affordable bars, and clubs running until dawn; best 7-11pm and on Friday-Saturday nights.
quote: Hongdae is one of the most popular neighborhoods in Seoul for shopping, street performances, cafes, nightlife, and youth culture ... known for its creative energy, buskers, indie roots

claim: Hongdae's live-music backbone includes Rolling Hall (30+ years as the heart of indie music) and Club Evans for live jazz, with street performances on the 'Red Road'-branded Walking Street.
quote: Rolling Hall celebrates over 30 years as the heart of indie music. Club Evans is the ultimate destination for live jazz ... The main thoroughfare, known as the 'Walking Street' (Eoulmadang-ro), is now officially managed under the brand 'Red Road.'

claim: Itaewon/Hannam is Seoul's most international district ('East meets West') with food from 50+ countries, the Leeum Samsung art museum in Hannam-dong, and the quieter hipster-cafe hill of Gyeongnidan-gil; skip if you only want 'authentic Korean.'
quote: Itaewon has food from 50+ countries ... Leeum Museum ... 'Samsung art museum' ... Gyeongnidan-gil ... features 'hipster cafes' and 'fusion restaurants' with 'local vibes' and is notably 'less crowded' ... skip if you 'only want authentic Korean experiences.'

claim: The Leeum Museum of Art in Hannam-dong, run by the Samsung Foundation of Culture, splits into a traditional Korean art wing and a contemporary art wing; admission is free but booking ahead is recommended.
quote: The Leeum Museum of Art is located in Hannam-dong, Yongsan District, Seoul, and is run by the Samsung Foundation of Culture. The museum consists of two parts, one of which houses traditional Korean art, the other contemporary art.

claim: Garosu-gil in Sinsa-dong is Gangnam's trendiest ginkgo-tree-lined street with high-end boutiques, K-beauty flagships (Sulwhasoo, Gentle Monster, Tamburins), and a boho-chic 'walk-in-the-park' K-drama vibe.
quote: Garosu-gil means 'tree-lined street' and is Gangnam's trendiest walking street, a ginkgo-lined avenue in Sinsa-dong ... flagship stores from Korean beauty brands like Sulwhasoo, Gentle Monster, and Tamburins ... a nostalgic walk-in-the-park vibe, just like in K-dramas

claim: Gangnam splits into COEX (huge underground mall with the free Starfield Library and K-Pop Square), Apgujeong (K-Star Road, luxury), Garosu-gil (boutiques and cafes), and Cheongdam-dong (ultra-luxury flagships and Michelin dining).
quote: four distinct sub-districts: COEX (SM TOWN retail, K-Pop Square LED screen), Apgujeong (K-Star Road installations, luxury shopping), Garosu-gil (independent boutiques and cafes), and Cheongdam-dong (ultra-luxury flagships and Michelin-starred dining) ... Starfield Library ... free to enter

claim: Myeongdong is Seoul's dense international-brand and K-beauty shopping strip, famed for cosmetic stores, beauty treatments, and a busy evening street-food scene, though it is very crowded and touristy.
quote: Myeongdong is the place for international brands and K-beauty. The popular Myeong-dong is known for its strip of cosmetic stores and beauty treatments.

claim: Insadong is the traditional-craft and art-gallery quarter near Bukchon, known for antique shops, galleries, and tea houses, while nearby Ikseon-dong is a renovated hanok-alley cafe-and-boutique district.
quote: Two Seoul Neighborhoods: Ikseon-dong & Bukchon Hanok Village

claim: Gwangjang Market, established 1905, is Korea's first permanent market; its 'Meokjagolmok' food alley draws most foreign visitors, with bindaetteok, yukhoe, and mayak gimbap as the three essentials, mayak gimbap around 3,000 KRW for ten pieces.
quote: The three essential items to eat at Gwangjang Market are Bindaetteok, Yukhoe, and Mayak Gimbap... Mayak Gimbap: Thumb-sized rice rolls with yellow pickled radish and sesame that cost around 3,000 KRW for ten pieces

claim: Seoul's signature dishes include double-fried Korean fried chicken (soy-garlic/spicy/plain), tteokbokki in sweet-spicy gochujang with fish cakes, samgyeopsal pork belly grilled tableside and wrapped in lettuce/perilla, and cold naengmyeon in icy beef broth; Sindang-dong is the birthplace of modern gochujang tteokbokki.
quote: Korean fried chicken is double-fried for an extraordinary crunch... Sindang-dong Tteokbokki Town near Sindang Station is considered the birthplace of the modern gochujang version of the dish... Thick-cut pork belly grilled at the table

claim: Pojangmacha are orange-tented street stalls appearing at night serving tteokbokki, odeng (fish cake skewers) and soju; sitting under one on a cold evening is a quintessential Korean experience.
quote: Pojangmacha are orange-tented street food stalls that appear at night and serve tteokbokki, odeng (fish cake skewers), and soju, with sitting under a pojangmacha tent on a cold evening being a quintessentially Korean experience.

claim: Makgeolli is Korea's oldest alcoholic drink (fermented rice, water, nuruk, 6-8% ABV), traditionally paired with savory jeon on rainy days; Anssi Makgeolli on Gyeongnidan-gil in Itaewon is the first traditional liquor bar in Korea to earn Michelin recognition, and Gwangjang has served makgeolli with bindaetteok for over a century.
quote: the traditional Korean belief is that makgeolli tastes best when it rains... paired with savory jeon... Anssi is the first traditional liquor bar in Korea to earn Michelin recognition

claim: Soju is roughly 16-20% ABV (half the strength of vodka); drinking etiquette requires pouring for elders with a hand on the forearm, and somaek (soju+beer) and chimaek (chicken+beer) are core social rituals.
quote: The alcohol content ranges from 16-20% ABV for standard brands — roughly half the strength of vodka... When pouring for someone older, place your left hand on your right forearm or elbow.

claim: Seoul has one of the world's most vibrant cafe scenes; Seongsu-dong, a former factory district, is now the most design-forward specialty-coffee neighborhood, while Ikseon-dong offers atmospheric cafes inside restored 1930s hanok serving traditional teas alongside espresso.
quote: This former factory district has transformed into Seoul's most design-forward coffee scene... Ikseon-dong in Jongno is Seoul's most atmospheric cafe neighborhood, set inside a dense cluster of restored hanok

claim: Seoul packs over 20,000 cafes into the capital, with Seongsu warehouse spaces (raw concrete, high ceilings) and Anguk/Ikseon hanok courtyard cafes; notable spots include Cafe Onion Seongsu, Daelim Changgo, London Bagel Museum and Fritz Coffee.
quote: over 20,000 cafes packed into the capital alone... old warehouse buildings converted into shopping areas and huge open-space cafes with raw concrete walls, high ceilings

claim: In 2026 soju sales have collapsed and youth binge drinking is down, making drinking strips quieter on weeknights than guidebooks suggest; makgeolli houses and craft-soju bars in Euljiro and Mangwon are now the better cultural gateway.
quote: soju sales have collapsed and youth binge drinking is down, making drinking strips quieter on weeknights than guidebooks suggest

claim: Hanbok rental in Seoul costs roughly 15,000-20,000 won and grants free entry to all five royal palaces plus hair styling and accessories.
quote: For 15,000-20,000 won — less than the price of a nice lunch — you get a complete hanbok outfit, Korean hair styling, accessories, and free entry to all five royal palaces.
note: Free palace entry requires wearing both top (jeogori) and bottom; regular palace ticket is only ~3,000 won.

claim: The 2026 Changdeokgung Moonlight Tour runs April 16-May 31, costs KRW 30,000, lasts ~100 minutes, and is sold exclusively on Creatrip starting April 2, 2026; foreigner sessions are limited and sell out fast.
quote: Changdeokgung Moonlight Tours will take place from April 16th – May 31st... The admission price to the Changdeokgung tour is KRW 30,000, with a limit of two tickets per buyer.
note: Reservation-only; bring foreign ID plus screenshot of voucher; check-in 20 min before.

claim: Jogyesa Temple in Insadong offers overnight templestay (1 night/2 days, ~50,000-100,000 KRW) and shorter day programs; popular slots fill up, so booking ~1 month ahead via eng.templestay.com is advised.
quote: Popular spots like Jogyesa fill up fast, so booking at least 1 month in advance is recommended through the Official Templestay Booking Website (eng.templestay.com). Prices are approximately 50,000 to 100,000 KRW per adult for a 2-day, 1-night stay.
note: Overnight program includes lotus lantern craft, monastic meals, optional 108 prostrations and 4:25am ceremony; foreigner 'One-day Zen Discovery' also available.

claim: Dragon Hill Spa in Yongsan is a 24-hour jjimjilbang charging roughly 15,000 won on weekends and 12,000 won on weekdays, with admission including spa access, sleeping rooms, clothes and towels.
quote: The entrance fee is 15,000 won per person on weekends and 12,000 won on weekdays... includes access to all spa locations and sleeping rooms, clothes and towels, as well as hairdryer and pillows.
note: Open 24/7; extra 1,000 won per hour after default duration.

claim: The National Museum of Korea in Yongsan has free admission to permanent exhibitions, open 10am-6pm most days and until 9pm on Wed and Sat.
quote: Admission is completely free to the permanent exhibitions. Only special exhibitions require entry fee... 10 a.m. – 6 p.m. (Sun.–Tue. & Thu.–Fri.) / 10 a.m. – 9 p.m. (Wed. & Sat.).
note: Located 137 Seobinggo-ro, Yongsan-gu; Ichon Station Exit 2.

claim: Leeum Museum of Art offers free permanent (traditional) collection by reservation, while special and contemporary exhibitions cost 18,000 KRW general admission (9,000 KRW discounted).
quote: The permanent traditional art collection is free, though reservations are required... general admission to the Leeum Samsung Museum of Art is priced at 18,000 KRW. There are discounted rates available for youth, teenagers, and seniors at 9,000 KRW.
note: Reservation required even for free collection; digital guides free in English.

claim: The War Memorial of Korea in Yongsan has free admission, open 9:30am-6:00pm and closed Mondays, near Itaewon.
quote: The War Memorial of Korea is open 9:30 AM - 6:00 PM, closed Mondays... Admission is free!
note: Last admission 5pm; plan 2-3 hours; located 29 Itaewon-ro, Yongsan-gu.

claim: The non-verbal Nanta cooking-themed percussion show in Myeongdong starts from ~37,500 won and plays at the UNESCO Building on Myeongdong-gil.
quote: Nanta show tickets in Seoul's Myeongdong start from ₩37,500... located at 3F, UNESCO Building, 26, Myeongdong-gil, Jung-gu, Seoul, Korea.
note: Blends traditional Korean rhythms with acrobatics; note Myeongdong Nanta Theater is distinct from Myeongdong Art Theater.

claim: Bukchon Hanok Village hosts traditional craft workshops (hanji paper, Korean knotwork, mother-of-pearl) running roughly 1-2 hours for 10,000-40,000 won, with materials and master instruction included.
quote: Expect ₩10,000-40,000 for 1-2 hour sessions, ₩60,000-150,000 for intensive programs, with prices including materials and master instruction.
note: Donglim Knot Workshop knotting passed down 4 generations; studios set in genuine hanok.

claim: Seoul K-pop dance experiences at HiKR Ground are ~2-hour beginner classes near Jonggak Station that teach hit choreography and produce an edited video shot in themed rooms.
quote: This 2-hour experience is perfect for anyone, even if you've never danced before, where you'll learn the highlight choreography of the latest K-pop hit in a private studio near Jonggak Station.
note: Small groups up to 6; HiKR Ground itself is a free tourism-center K-pop attraction with music-video-set photo zones.

claim: Banpo Bridge's Moonlight Rainbow Fountain (Guinness world's longest bridge fountain) runs free shows mid-March to October, starting around sunset, every half hour for ~20 minutes; Banpo Hangang Park offers free picnics, cycling and walking trails.
quote: You can catch the Moonlight Rainbow Fountain show from Mid-March to October... performances scheduled several times each evening. The shows typically begin at sunset and run every half hour, with each performance lasting about 20 minutes.

claim: Banpo Hangang Park is reached via subway Line 3, 7 or 9 to Express Bus Terminal Station, Exit 8-1/8-2, and the fountain show and park are free.
quote: Banpo Bridge Rainbow Fountain

claim: Seoul in June 2026 is early summer and pre-monsoon: daytime highs around 24.8°C early month rising to 26.1°C late month, lows 15-18°C, humidity 66-81%, with the monsoon typically arriving only in the last week of June.
quote: in the early part of the month, highs average 24.8°C | 76.6°F and lows 14.9°C | 58.8°F... By the end of the month, highs average 26.1°C | 79°F, while lows fall to 18.2°C | 64.8°F.

claim: June rain in Korea is intermittent rather than constant (heavy continuous rain comes in July), and June has the longest daylight hours of the year.
quote: Heavy, continuous rain is more common in July, and rain in June is intermittent, not constant... the longest days of the year in Korea are also in June.

claim: June 2026 Seoul events include the MY PACE Hangang Triathlon (Jun 5-7, Ttukseom), the free SPO Riverside Concert with fireworks (Jun 13, Yeouido Hangang Park), and the Seoul Gugak Festival of traditional music (Jun 19, Banpo Hangang Park).
quote: 2026 SPO Riverside Concert (June 13) at Yeouido Hangang Park. A 'free outdoor concert' with 'classical masterpieces and a dazzling fireworks display.'... 2026 Seoul Gugak Festival (June 19) at Banpo Hangang Park.

claim: Other June 2026 Seoul programming includes the Car-Free Jamsugyo Festival on the first two Sundays of June at Jamsugyo Bridge/Banpo Park, the Seoul World DJ Festival (Jun 13-14), and the Seoul Outdoor Library popping up Friday-Sunday across the city including Seoul Plaza.
quote: The Car-Free Jamsugyo Festival takes place during the first two Sundays in June along the Jamsugyo Bridge and within Banpo Hangang Park... The annual Seoul Outdoor Library opens throughout June every Friday to Sunday.

claim: Seoul Sky in Lotte World Tower (554.5m building, observation deck at 497m, 3rd-highest in the world) has a 118th-floor glass-floor Sky Deck and river views, while cheaper N Seoul Tower (236.7m on Namsan) sits in green parkland, is less crowded and is known for Love Locks.
quote: Lotte World Tower is 554.5 metres tall... The main observation deck at Lotte World Tower is located at 497 meters, the 3rd highest in the world... On the 118th floor Sky Deck at Seoul Sky, you can walk out onto transparent glass floors.

claim: The Seoul City Wall (Hanyangdoseong) runs 18.6km over Bugaksan, Naksan, Namsan and Inwangsan; the easy Naksan Mountain Trail (Hyehwamun to Heunginjimun) is 2.1km/~1hr over the 124m hill, the lowest of Seoul's four inner mountains.
quote: The Naksan Mountain Trail (Hyehwamun Gate to Heunginjimun Gate), 2.1km, 1 hr. This hiking trail passes Naksan Mountain (124m), the lowest mountain of Seoul's four inner mountains and is a relatively easy trail due to its gentle slope.

claim: The full Seoul City Wall can be hiked in 8-10 hours starting early, but summer walks are discouraged due to 30°C+ heat and the late-July monsoon; the Namsan section gives the most panoramic views.
quote: One-day completion: Starting early morning (7 AM) allows fit adults to complete all 18.6km in 8-10 hours... Skip summer Hanyangdoseong walks. Extreme heat (30°C+) and monsoon season... create dangerous conditions.

claim: Bukhansan's Baegundae Peak (836.5m, Seoul's highest summit) is a moderately hard ~7km, 4-6hr round hike reached via the Ui-Sinseol line to Bukhansan Ui Station, with a final exposed 300m rock-face section using fixed metal ropes.
quote: Baegundae Peak, at 836.5m is the highest peak in Bukhansan National Park... The final 300 meters... involves ascending a steep rock face using fixed metal ropes and handrails.

claim: Popular Seoul day trips include the DMZ/JSA (guided, ~₩55,000-85,000, JSA needs 72-hour advance booking and is often closed for security), Nami Island via early ITX train to Gapyeong, and Suwon's 5.7km Hwaseong Fortress (60 min on Metro Line 1, ~₩1,750), best done on weekdays.
quote: The DMZ is the most expensive day trip at ₩55,000-85,000 because you need a guided tour. Panmunjom and JSA tours require a minimum 72-hour advance booking... Hwaseong Fortress... stretches 5.7 kilometres.

claim: Bukchon Hanok Village's 'Eight Scenic Views' sit between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces and include the Bukchon Observatory hill viewpoint in Gahoe-dong and the Samcheong-dong stone stairway, framing traditional rooftops against the modern skyline.
quote: The Eight Scenic Views of Bukchon can be found at the Bukchon Hanok Village between Gyeongbokgung Palace and Changdeokgung Palace... a view from the hill at Gahoe-dong (Bukchon Observatory)... and the stone stairway at Samcheong-dong.

claim: Ihwa Mural Village is a quieter hillside outdoor-art alternative to Bukchon, reached from Hyehwa Station Exit 2, where residents still live and visitors are asked to keep noise down.
quote: Ihwa Mural Village Seoul: What To See, Where To Go and How To Visit Respectfully

claim: AREX Express from Incheon Airport to Seoul Station is non-stop, ~43 min from T1 (51 min from T2), costing about 11,000 KRW (cheaper online); the all-stop train runs every 5-10 min, takes ~59 min and costs up to ~5,350 KRW.
quote: Travel Time: 43 minutes (from T1) / 51 minutes (from T2)... The 2026 AREX Fare is 11,000 KRW for Express... all-stop fares are up to 5,350 KRW depending on destination

claim: A taxi from Incheon Airport to central Seoul takes 60-80 minutes and costs roughly 65,000-100,000 KRW including the ~7,900 KRW airport expressway toll, with international taxis about 20% more.
quote: estimated fare of 65,000–100,000 KRW (includes toll fees)... An additional toll for Incheon Int'l Airport Expressway (₩7,900)... International taxis are 20 percent more expensive

claim: Airport limousine/buses from Incheon to Seoul cost roughly 5,000-15,000 KRW and take about 60-80 minutes depending on traffic and destination.
quote: Tickets are KRW 5,000 to 15,000 and travel time is approximately 60 to 80 minutes, depending on traffic and destination

claim: Gimpo Airport (GMP) is inside the city, so AREX/subway reaches Seoul Station in ~20 min and Gangnam/COEX in ~38 min for ~1,550 KRW, far quicker than Incheon's 50km island location.
quote: Travel from Gimpo International Airport to Seoul Station takes about 20 minutes... Time: 25 mins to Yeouido... 38 mins to Gangnam/COEX... Price: ~1,550 KRW

claim: The Climate Card tourist pass costs 5,000 (1-day), 8,000 (2-day), 10,000 (3-day) and 15,000 (5-day) KRW for unlimited Seoul subway and city buses, but excludes bike-share and does not let you board AREX at the Incheon terminals (you can only alight there).
quote: 1-day Pass: KRW 5,000... 2-day Pass: KRW 8,000... 3-day Pass: KRW 10,000... 5-day Pass: KRW 15,000... you cannot take the train at T1 and T2

claim: The short-term Climate Card tourist pass requires no Korean phone number, ARC or online account, unlike resident monthly passes.
quote: The short-term Tourist Pass (1-7 days) does not require a Korean phone number, an Alien Registration Card (ARC), or any online account

claim: A reusable T-money card costs ~3,000-5,000 KRW at convenience stores and deducts ~1,550 KRW per subway ride; it works nationwide (Seoul, Busan, Jeju), making it better than the Seoul-only Climate Card for travel beyond the capital.
quote: You buy the physical card for roughly ₩3,000 to ₩5,000 at any convenience store. Every time you ride the subway, ₩1,550 gets deducted... a T-Money card works in Seoul, Busan, Jeju Island, and rural towns

claim: Citizens of 67 visa-waiver countries (incl. US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, Japan) are temporarily exempt from K-ETA through December 31, 2026 and can enter visa-free for stays up to 90 days for tourism.
quote: extended the temporary exemption from the Korea Electronic Travel Authorization (K-ETA) requirement... until December 31, 2026... A visa is not required for stays 90 days or less for business or tourism

claim: K-ETA-exempt travelers must instead complete an e-Arrival Card (digital form) within 3 days before each arrival to Korea.
quote: An e-Arrival Card is a trip-specific digital form that must be completed within 3 days before every arrival and is mandatory for all travelers who do not have a K-ETA

claim: Google Maps gives unreliable walking/transit directions in Seoul due to Korea's map-data export restrictions, so Naver Map and KakaoMap (both with English support and real-time transit) are the reliable navigation apps; Google's high-precision data export was only conditionally approved in May 2026.
quote: South Korea has a unique law restricting the export of detailed mapping data... Google Maps' turn-by-turn navigation... is often wrong or missing entirely in Seoul... government conditionally approved Google's export of high-precision map data... as of May 2026

claim: Solo short-trip travelers are best served by an eSIM (instant QR activation, one-time cost), while groups or heavy/streaming users benefit from pocket WiFi with unlimited data; all three carriers (KT, SKT, LG U+) sell prepaid unlimited SIMs at Incheon Airport.
quote: all three major carriers (KT, SK Telecom, and LG U+) at Incheon Airport... offer prepaid SIMs with unlimited data... eSIM can be more cost-effective for travelers who plan to stay... for a shorter period

claim: Myeongdong is the most practical base for first-timers being central, walkable and well-connected, but is crowded and tourist-heavy; Insadong/Jongno offers traditional charm near the palaces; Hongdae is cheapest with the best nightlife and a direct AREX link; Gangnam is newer, larger-roomed and more upscale.
quote: Myeongdong is the most practical choice for first-timers, being central, walkable, well-connected by subway... Hongdae is the cheapest area... plus the most affordable accommodation and a direct AREX connection to Incheon Airport... Gangnam district's hotels are newer

claim: A standard 2-day Seoul skeleton spends Day 1 on traditional Seoul (Gyeongbokgung Palace with 10am guard change, walk to Bukchon Hanok Village, lunch in Insadong, Myeongdong night market from ~5pm) and Day 2 on modern Seoul (N Seoul Tower, cafes, K-beauty, shopping), leaving evening slots open.
quote: Start your day with a visit to Gyeongbokgung Palace... changing of the guard ceremony at 10 AM... walk to the nearby Bukchon Hanok Village... Head to Insadong... Visit the night market in Myeongdong... starting at around 5pm
